title: Clara and the False Fanfare
markdown:
In the old theatre the velvet curtains sagged like tired eyelids, and rehearsal buzzed with ambition wrestling terror.

Clara the cat, ebony fur, paws made for pianos, sat at the grand. Rehearsal pianist. Emerald eyes, usually calm pools, assessed the agitated room. She knew a quiet useful truth: this fiendish sonata wanted practice, not fanfare.

The room, alas, adored a dazzling fib. It preferred the glitter of effortless mastery to the honest grind. A nervous rustle went through the students. Clara’s whiskers trembled. Her truth might drown. Expectation sat on small shoulders.

This is fear, she thought. What if it is not enough?

Rhun Butterfield strode forth, ego inflated like a blimp. “This sonata is a mere trifle! A charming melody for discerning ears!” He beamed, a peacock for an unseen crowd, grin threatening his face.

Jules the raven, stage manager, watched from a high rafter, practicality in black. He cocked his head. “Rhun. The final movement. A labyrinth of trills and arpeggios.”

“Labyrinth?” Rhun scoffed, a tiny explosion in a teacup. “Code for unplayed by the uninspired.” A sly smirk at Clara. “A demonstration, feline maestro. A flourish. A whisker’s worth of effort.”

So it began. Rhun launched a cascade that, to untrained ears, sounded sensational, a firework of fingers in a room hungry for sparks. Paws a blur. Clara, whose hearing went past training, caught the rot under the gilt: a missed beat where the labyrinth turned, a flattened chord that should have lifted the last movement like a curtain. The music, meant to soar, hobbled. Dust moved in the stage-light. The room erupted anyway. They wanted the expensive lie, and they paid in applause.

Clara’s paws clenched. She yearned to cry that he was rushing. Dread of spoiling his parade held her. Her competence felt suddenly thin. Rhun bowed far larger than the playing and radiated smugness.

Then, on a polished silver tray left by an attendant, a reflection: not the virtuoso the room adored, but a nervous boy with an unconfident wince. The tray told on the lie.

Jules swooped, landed soft, nudged her with a wing. “He is skilled at sounding good. Sounding good is not being good. Shiny apple. Worm inside.”

That was the prod. She looked at Rhun preening, at anxious faces tethered to the illusion. The useful truth—practice, honest effort—was too precious to abandon.

“Rhun,” Clara said, steady, a clean note through false cheer. “That is an excellent notion, which is why I must question it. This sonata is no trifle. It demands respect. Patience. Admitting we have not mastered it, then working to learn. A clear head and a steady paw. Not merely a flurry.”

Rhun blinked. The room held its breath. Sincerity landed harder than bombast.

“I will remain,” she declared—bold, for a cat who cherished naps. Extra hours flickered dread; conviction burned brighter. “I will rehearse it with you until every note sings true. Honesty. Effort. Sometimes the path is simply hard work. No more dazzling falsehoods. Agreed?”

When she offered a helping paw instead of a verdict, and spent the rest she had wanted, the room began to unclench. The need to appear flawless thinned like mist. The lie looked suddenly exhausting, a castle of spun sugar.

Rhun, met with aid not scorn, looked at Clara, at the tray, at the faces. He swallowed. A small genuine smile. Bravado leaked away. “All right, Clara. Let’s practise it properly. No more show. Just playing.”

The room, no longer performing certainty, breathed. Careful practice filled the air, a better melody than bravado. Jules, from the rafter, clicked his beak once, which in raven was applause, and Clara set her paws on the keys as if they were ordinary work, which they were, and began again from the movement that had pretended to be easy.
audience: young adults aged 16-18, teen anthology entry
